title: RISE: Rule-Driven SQL Dialect Translation via Query Reduction
migration_kind: DIA (PostgreSQL→MySQL on TPC-DS, 99 queries; PostgreSQL→Oracle stored procedures on SQLProcBench, 44 queries); not tagged LEGACY
track: ICSE 2026 Research Track (per the ACM reference in the file)
llm_role: Proposed technique (RISE uses an LLM to reduce queries and to translate the reduced queries, from which it derives translation rules); LLM baselines (LLMTranslator GPT-4o/DeepSeek-V3, CrackSQL) along with 3 rule-based tools (SQLGlot, SQLines, jOOQ); LLMs are also the subject of the empirical study in §2
oracle_origin: O-b: execution on the target DBMS (execution/syntax errors); O-f: running the original query on the source DBMS with the benchmark's data, comparing results and DB state (running the original system); O-i: the authors manually reviewed the queries with matching results. O-f is also the validity check inside RISE (§3.1).
multiple_oracles_same_outputs: Yes. Table 1 (143 queries): LLMTranslator_GPT has 7 syntax errors and 12 non-equivalent, accuracy 86.71%; LLMTranslator_DS has 9 syntax errors and 16 non-equivalent, accuracy 82.52%. The number of cases rejected at the manual review step is not reported separately. Table 2 reports only aggregate accuracy (RISE 97.98% TPC-DS, 100% SQLProcBench).
stated_limitations: “relying solely on the execution results of DBMSs cannot ensure complete accuracy” (§5.2; example: the '||' operator returns empty results on both DBMSs and so slips through)
evidence:
“execute the translated query on the target DBMS and compare … the source DBMS” (§2.1.3)
“For queries with consistent results … manual verification to confirm semantic equivalence” (§2.1.3)
“stores different database states … query that is intended to modify the database state” (§3.1)
“translate queries from PostgreSQL to MySQL … stored procedures from PostgreSQL to Oracle” (§4.2)
“both DBMSs returned empty results, causing RISE to mistakenly conclude … semantically equivalent” (§5.2)

title: SmartC2Rust: Iterative, Feedback-Driven C-to-Rust Translation via Large Language Models for Safety and Equivalence
migration_kind: XL (C→Rust). Not LEGACY (the C is called 'legacy C code', but it is not a legacy system in the COBOL/mainframe sense).
llm_role: Proposed technique (Claude 3.7 Sonnet in a translate–repair loop); baselines: C2Rust, Crown, Laertes (rule-based), C2SaferRust (C2Rust + LLM), plus a comparison with Syzygy on zopfli; GPT-4o and Gemini Pro 1.5 backends also tried.
oracles: O-b, O-c, O-d, O-f (secondary: rate of macros preserved, close to O-a)
oracle_origin: O-b: rustc/cargo; O-c: existing tests from the repo ('built-in') and from third parties ('provided'); some tests written manually by the authors ('created'); O-d: for non-standalone programs, a C test program is written and then translated to Rust along with the code; O-f: running the original C version to obtain outputs/call traces as the reference, then comparing with the Rust version. The same test set serves both as feedback in the loop and as the final measure.
multiple_oracles_same_outputs: Yes. Table 4: SmartC2Rust 0 compilation errors vs 100% tests; C2Rust 9 errors vs 80%±30; Crown 253 errors vs 35%±47; Laertes 13 errors vs 80%; C2SaferRust 9 errors vs 80%. Ablation: removing the flow comparison → test pass 23.3%; random order/no summary/fixed-file repair → compilation 28.5%/32.3%/12.4%; GPT-4o compilation 34.3%, Gemini 12.4%.
stated_limitations: The LLM is "simplifying and rewriting the code just to make the test cases pass" (§6 Scalability)
evidence:
"executes both the original and translated code … compares the execution results" (§2.2)
"results from the C golden implementation … compares them with the actual execution results" (§4 Implementation)
"'built-in' (from original repository), 'created' (manually developed …), or 'provided' (from third-party repositories)" (§4 Dataset)
"not standalone, we rewrite the developer-written test cases even if they exist" (§4)
"All Rust code … error-free … 0 compilation errors and 100 % passing rate" (§5.2)
